entries.title: ipc
entries.summary: How processes cooperate: signals, pipes, shared memory, messages.
entries.syntax: signals   pipes   shared memory   message passing
entries.description: Independent processes do not affect each other; **cooperating** processes do, to share information, speed up a job or split it into modules. They need **interprocess communication (IPC)**. To warn about an event: **signals** (`kill`) and **semaphores**. To transfer data: **pipes** (a one-way channel, usually between parent and child), **shared memory** (a region both can read and write, with no help from the kernel after it is set up) and **message passing** (`send` / `receive`, the kernel moves the data and the processes do not share memory; it also works between machines).

entries.title: shared-memory
entries.summary: A memory region that two processes can both use.
entries.description: The kernel maps one segment of memory into the address space of several processes. Afterwards they communicate simply by reading and writing it; the kernel does not intervene, so the processes decide the layout of the data and must **synchronise** their accesses themselves (semaphores, mutexes). The calls are `shmget` (create or find the segment), `shmat` / `shmdt` (attach / detach it) and `shmctl` (control or remove it). Threads share memory without any of this, because they live in one process.
mistakes: Forgetting that shared memory without synchronisation has the same race conditions as threads.

entries.title: message-passing
entries.summary: send and receive: communication without shared memory.
entries.description: Processes exchange messages with two operations, `send` and `receive`, and the system hides where the other side is. It suits processes on different machines. The communication can be **blocking** (synchronous): the sender waits until the message is received, the receiver waits until a message arrives; or **non-blocking** (asynchronous): the sender goes on at once, the receiver gets a message or an empty answer. Compared with shared memory it is easier to get right, but every message passes through the kernel.

entries.title: pipe
entries.summary: A one-way channel between processes (a pair of file descriptors).
entries.description: Creates a pipe and stores two descriptors in `fd`: `fd[0]` is the end you **read** from and `fd[1]` the end you **write** to. A pipe is one-way: data written at one end comes out at the other, in order. `read` **blocks** while the pipe is empty, and returns `0` (end of file) only when **every** descriptor of the write end, in every process, has been closed. A child created with `fork` inherits both descriptors, so each process must `close` the end it does not use, as soon as it can. For a conversation in both directions use two pipes. `fdopen` turns an end into a `FILE *`; `dup2` connects an end to stdin or stdout before an `exec` (how a shell builds `a | b`).
mistakes: Not closing the unused ends: the reader never sees the end of file and hangs.
Creating the pipe AFTER the `fork`: parent and child then have different pipes.
Reading more than you wrote and printing the buffer as a string without adding the `'\0'`.

entries.title: signals
entries.summary: Notifications sent to a process: SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGKILL, SIGUSR1...
entries.syntax: SIGINT 2   SIGKILL 9   SIGUSR1 10   SIGTERM 15   SIGCHLD 17   SIGSTOP 19
entries.description: A signal tells a process that something happened. It acts like an interrupt: the process stops what it is doing, runs the **handler** for that signal, and goes on. For each signal a process can **ignore** it (`SIG_IGN`), keep the **default action** (`SIG_DFL`: most signals end the process) or install **its own handler**. The important ones: `SIGINT` (Ctrl+C), `SIGTERM` (polite request to end, the default of `kill`), `SIGKILL` (kills at once: cannot be caught or ignored), `SIGSTOP` (stops the process, also cannot be caught; Ctrl+Z sends `SIGTSTP`, which can), `SIGUSR1` and `SIGUSR2` (free for the programmer, default: end the process), `SIGCHLD` (a child ended: default is to ignore it), `SIGALRM` (an `alarm` expired), `SIGPIPE` (write to a pipe nobody reads) and `SIGSEGV` (invalid memory access).
mistakes: Trying to catch `SIGKILL` or `SIGSTOP`: it is not allowed.
Using `printf` in a handler: it is not safe (use `write`).

entries.title: signal
entries.summary: Choose what a process does when it receives a signal.
entries.description: Sets the action for the signal `signum`: `SIG_IGN` (ignore it), `SIG_DFL` (the default action) or a function `void handler(int sig)` of yours, which receives the signal number. It returns the previous action (or `SIG_ERR`). A handler stays installed for next time on Linux. Handlers inherited through `fork` stay; `exec` puts caught signals back to default. Inside a handler do as little as possible: set a flag (`volatile sig_atomic_t`), or call `write`, `_exit`... (functions that are *async-signal-safe*); `printf` and `malloc` are not.
mistakes: Installing the handler after the signal may already have arrived (install it BEFORE `fork`).
Relying on a signal being delivered once per `kill`: several equal signals can merge into one.

entries.title: kill
entries.summary: Send a signal to a process.
entries.description: Sends the signal `sig` to the process with the given pid (also the `kill` command: `kill -USR1 1234`). Returns `0`, or `-1` on error (no such process, no permission). With `sig` equal to `0` nothing is sent: it only checks that the process exists. Sending a signal to a child that has not yet installed its handler can kill it: install the handler before `fork`.
mistakes: Passing the arguments the other way round: it is `kill(pid, signal)`.
Using `kill(0, sig)`, which signals the whole process group.

entries.title: raise
entries.description: Equivalent to `kill(getpid(), sig)`. The signal is delivered before `raise` returns, so the handler has already run when the next line executes (in a single-threaded program).
entries.example:
signal(SIGUSR1, handler);
raise(SIGUSR1);   /* handler runs here */

entries.title: pause
entries.description: Suspends the process until a signal is caught; after the handler returns, `pause` returns `-1` (with `errno` set to `EINTR`). Beware of the **lost wakeup**: if the signal arrives between your test of a flag and the call to `pause`, you wait forever. The reliable tools are `sigsuspend`, or a loop with `sleep`; in simple programs make sure the other side starts late enough.
mistakes: Writing `while (!flag) pause();` and thinking it is perfectly safe.

entries.title: alarm
entries.summary: Ask for a SIGALRM after some seconds.
entries.description: Arranges for the process to receive `SIGALRM` in the given number of seconds, and returns the seconds left of a previous alarm. `alarm(0)` cancels it. There is only one alarm per process: a new call replaces the old one. If nobody handles `SIGALRM` the default action ends the process.
mistakes: Forgetting to install the handler: the process is killed by the alarm.
